card.thesis: Large institutional managers who file Form 13F disclose share-count changes with a ~45-day lag, so by the time a new or materially increased position is public the manager is often still mid-build: 13F filers of this size (multi-billion-dollar books) cannot fill a real position in a single session without moving the tape, so a disclosed NEW or ADD (measured strictly in shares, never in dollar value, so a repricing is never mistaken for a purchase) frequently reflects buying pressure that continues for weeks or months after the filing becomes public, both from the manager finishing the trade and from other participants who watch 13F disclosures and follow. The seller on the other side of that continued buying is typically a retail holder or an index fund forced to trade at whatever price prevails -- neither is pricing in the institutional accumulation the filing just revealed. This card does not trade the 13F signal directly (the filing is stale by 45+ days and by itself says nothing about timing); it uses cross-manager 13F conviction only to pick a universe of names multiple institutions were accumulating as of the last filing legally visible before this card's eligible window opens, then requires the market's own price action -- a name in an established uptrend that has just pushed to a fresh short-term high -- to confirm the accumulation is still live before risking capital. What is expected to go wrong: every name that survived to the tradeable universe below is a mega-cap technology / semiconductor name (see memo -- this is what 13F conviction resolves to once CUSIP-to-ticker resolution and cross-manager agreement are both applied), so this card is a concentrated bet on continued AI/mega-cap-tech leadership. It is expected to underperform badly in a rotation out of that theme (value/small-cap leadership, a mega-cap-tech-specific drawdown, or a market where breadth broadens away from these exact names) even if the broad market holds up, and the 200-day trend filter will keep it flat-footed at the start of any sharp reversal since it only reduces exposure after the long-term average has already rolled over.
card.entry: close > sma(200) and close crosses_above sma(20)

card.thesis: This engine cannot express relative strength: entry and exit are evaluated per symbol against that symbol's own bars, with no cross-sectional comparison, so there is no way to buy 'the strongest semiconductor name' or trade a spread. What this card actually does is apply one absolute condition -- close above its own 50-day average with RSI(14) between 55 and 80, i.e. a confirmed, non-extreme uptrend -- identically to a 9-name cyclical-semiconductor universe (NVDA AMD MU INTC MRVL AVGO TSM QCOM SOXX), and cap concurrent holdings at 3 of 9. That cap is the only 'rotation' logic available: the mechanism is that semiconductor demand and AI-capex cycles tend to move the whole group together and to persist for quarters rather than days, so entering only into names already confirmed in trend, and exiting on trend break or momentum fade, should keep capital on the right side of the cycle more often than not, while the cap prevents any single session from committing to more than 3 names at once. I measured pairwise daily-return correlation across these 9 names over the trailing ~253 sessions through 2026-02-13: mean 0.589, range 0.286 (INTC vs AVGO) to 0.824 (SOXX vs TSM). That is high -- this is a concentrated sector bet dressed as a 3-of-9 rotation, not a diversified basket, and I am not pretending otherwise. It is not a coin-flip between one name and nothing, though: breadth genuinely varies session to session under the proposed filter (median 4 of 9 names qualifying; at least 4 qualify on 50.6% of sessions, at least 6 on 21.3%), so the cap binds and actually forces a choice often enough to matter. When more than 3 names qualify on the same session, the broker fills entries in the fixed order the universe list is written -- alphabetical here -- not by any measure of relative strength, momentum magnitude, or liquidity. That is an arbitrary tiebreak, not a 'buy the leader' mechanism, and the card cannot do better than that. On the other side of these trades: momentum/trend traders who initiated the move earlier and are already positioned before this rule confirms it; mean-reversion sellers who fade strength too early inside a still-intact uptrend and get run over; and dip-buyers in choppy or declining regimes who buy bottoms this rule cannot see coming and will instead get chopped by.
card.entry: close > sma(50) and rsi(14) > 55 and rsi(14) < 80

card.thesis: A 200-day moving average is a slow proxy for whether the marginal buyer still controls the tape. Structural forced sellers -- pensions and mandate-bound funds de-risking after a sustained decline, and levered holders forced out by drawdown -- keep supplying stock into a market that has been falling for months, which is exactly what 'price below its own 200-day average' detects; staying out during that condition avoids selling into their hands and re-enters only once buyers have re-established control on a monthly-to-quarterly timescale. Applying the same filter independently across four largely uncorrelated exposures (US equities SPY, international developed equities EFA, long Treasuries TLT, gold GLD) means one asset's trend break does not force the whole book to cash: in a rate-driven equity bear, the flight-to-quality bid that keeps bonds and gold trending up is a countercyclical buyer the strategy rides while equities are excluded, so exposure and return both keep coming from somewhere. Pre-registered failure regime: a sideways, choppy, low-trend market has no edge for this filter and pays repeated whipsaw entries/stop-outs against a benchmark that simply sits still; and a regime where every asset class de-rates together (a simultaneous equity-and-bond bear, e.g. a rate shock) removes nearly the whole book to cash-like exposure at once, leaving the strategy flat while a buy-and-hold benchmark may partially recover before the filter re-engages.
card.entry: close > sma(200)

card.display_name: Band Reversion — Broad Market & Sector ETFs
card.thesis: Mechanism: a close below the 20-day, 2-stdev Bollinger lower band while price still sits above its 200-day SMA is disproportionately forced, price-insensitive selling inside an intact uptrend -- stop-loss cascades from levered/margin accounts, mechanical VaR/vol-target de-risking by risk-parity and vol-targeting funds reacting to a spike in realised volatility, and index/ETF authorized-participant redemption flow. None of that flow carries a fundamental view; the 200-day trend filter is the proxy for 'nothing structural has changed yet'. The counterparty on my entry is that forced seller. Once the flow clears, price tends to revert toward the 20-day mean as valuation-insensitive rebalancers (funds trading back to target weight) and short-term dip buyers step back in; my exit sells into that reversion at the middle band, before it can be told apart from a genuine trend resumption. Pre-registered failure regime: a fast, deep, sustained decline where the 200-day SMA (which is slow by construction) has not yet turned down before the crash accelerates -- GFC's Sep-Oct 2008 leg and COVID's Feb-Mar 2020 leg are the two candidates. In that regime the entry keeps firing on 'dips' that are actually the first third of a much larger decline, the 20-day reversion does not arrive inside the 20-day hold, and positions exit on the stop or the time cap at a loss, repeatedly, until the 200-day SMA finally rolls over and the filter shuts the strategy off -- likely after most of the damage in that leg is already done.
card.entry: close < bb_lower(20,2.0) and close > sma(200)

card.thesis: A close that breaks above a confirmed multi-week swing high forces two groups to act, not just one: short sellers who sold into the old resistance are now underwater and mechanically buy to cover, and systematic trend/breakout funds (CTA-style N-day-high rules are a large, well-documented share of managed-futures and momentum flow) generate a fresh buy signal on the same event. Both are non-discretionary, price-triggered flows, which is why a break of an established range tends to keep going for a while rather than immediately mean-revert -- the buying is not opinion, it is a rule firing. The sma(200) trend filter restricts entries to sectors already in a primary uptrend, because a break of a local high inside a primary downtrend is disproportionately a bear-market rally, not a fresh trend. What I expect to go wrong: a grinding, broad-based bear (bear-2022-style) still produces some sector-level breakout signals -- sectors do not top in lockstep -- and those are precisely the trades that get overrun when the broader decline catches up, so I expect this card's worst window to be a bear regime, not a crash. See memo for the measured entry-frequency-by-window breakdown that grounds this.
card.entry: close crosses_above swing_high(20) and close > sma(200)

card.display_name: G - Range expansion: beat the blind window
card.thesis: A true-range day 1.5x its own ATR(14) is the market printing new information faster than participants can absorb it -- an earnings reaction, a guidance change, a sector-wide repricing. When that expansion day also closes above open and above the 50-day trend, the imbalance is more likely a repricing that continues than a one-day panic that mean-reverts: momentum research (e.g. post-earnings drift) shows large-surprise days keep drifting for weeks because slow-moving capital (index funds, institutions with review cycles, retail attention) re-rates the name over days rather than instantly. The counterparty is whoever sells into that expansion bar at the old price because they have not yet re-priced the new information, or is forced to sell into the move on a stop or a mandate -- both hand the follow-through to whoever holds after the bar closes. This is genuinely a volatility-discipline: the trigger is range relative to ATR, not a moving-average cross or an oversold oscillator, so it is selecting for the size of the move as well as its direction. The engine's structural weakness for this discipline is that stop_loss_pct and position_pct are single numbers with no per-symbol ATR scaling, so I measured ATR-to-price across the full 43-symbol universe through 2026-02-13 and it spans roughly 0.04% (SGOV) to 10.5% (OKLO) -- a ~260x range in which one stop cannot fit both ends. Rather than accept that mismatch, I built a 12-symbol universe (NVDA, AMD, MU, INTC, MRVL, DELL, AVGO, TSLA, COIN, NET, SNOW, PLTR) whose trailing-year ATR/price ratios cluster tightly between 3.68% and 5.98% (mean 4.76%, max/min ratio 1.6x, versus 260x for the full list) -- comparable-enough volatility that one stop and one size are a defensible approximation rather than a silent lie the thesis pretends isn't there. I deliberately excluded the very-low-vol cash/bond/gold names (SGOV, AGG, GLD, SCHD -- ATR/price under 2%, where a 10% stop is nearly un-hittable noise) and the extreme-vol small caps (IREN, APLD, OKLO, NBIS, BE, CRDO, SNDK -- ATR/price above 6.5%, where a 10% stop is routine chop) for the same reason. ATR/price also persists strongly in this universe (lag-1 autocorrelation 0.94-0.99, lag-5 0.79-0.94 across all 43 names, measured through 2026-02-13) -- volatility regimes here are not one-day noise, they cluster for weeks, which is what makes an ATR-relative trigger meaningful rather than arbitrary.
card.entry: high - low > atr(14) * 1.5 and close > open and close > sma(50)

card.thesis: Institutional flow into AI/cloud-infrastructure leaders re-rates them in slow, multi-week waves, not single days: a fund building a position over weeks pushes the medium-term average through the long-term one, and that crossover is a public, mechanical signal other trend-following capital reacts to next, extending the move further than any one participant intended. On the design-window history of these 12 names, once close > sma(200) is already established and ema(20) crosses above ema(50) -- a fresh acceleration inside a standing uptrend, not a bottom-pick -- the resulting move has a median duration of roughly 3-4 weeks and stretches past two months at the 75th percentile (NVDA's longest such run reached 256 sessions, MSFT's 169, TSM's 189). The other side of this trade is whoever sells into that strength: value-discipline holders trimming into a re-rate, and short sellers pressing a name that 'already ran too far' -- both wrong, on average, while the wave is still building. I tested a fixed take-profit and a fast rule exit against simply riding the position to a stop or a genuine trend break, on this same entry: capping gains at 8-30% cut mean per-signal return to 2-9%, and a fast 20-day-EMA exit (even with a 3-day confirmation filter) cut it to 3-5% and win rate to 42-49% by whipsawing out of live trends on ordinary pullbacks. Letting the position run to a stop, a 200-day trend-break, or a 180-day backstop produced roughly triple the aggregate return of either capped variant, at the cost of a median trade near breakeven-to-slightly-negative -- this strategy's edge is concentrated in a minority of large winners, which is exactly what a take-profit would have amputated. It is deliberately not diversified across volatility regimes: the universe was chosen so one stop and one position size fit all 12 names reasonably rather than being tuned to any single one.
card.entry: ema(20) crosses_above ema(50) and close > sma(200)

card.thesis: In liquid, heavily-owned AI/semiconductor-cycle names, a short, sharp price dislocation -- a 2-3 session air-pocket severe enough to push RSI(3) under 15 while price pierces a tight 10-day Bollinger band -- is usually forced-flow selling (stop cascades, options-dealer delta hedging, single-headline overreaction) rather than a genuine repricing of the business, and forced flow exhausts itself in days, not weeks. On this universe over 2021-02-13 through 2026-02-13, 306 such dislocations resolved (price closing back above ema(5)) in a median of 4 sessions and a mean of 4.4, with only 4.2% still unresolved after 10 sessions -- so the reversion this trades is fast almost every time it happens at all, which is exactly the profile a tight max_hold_days is built for. The other side of this trade is whoever sold into the panic at the worst print: momentum/CTA systematic sellers extending a move 1-3 sessions past where fundamentals justify, and retail stop-outs clearing into thin liquidity. Exiting on the first close back above ema(5) -- not waiting for a full return to the 10- or 20-day mean -- is deliberate: in the same sample the median bounce at that first ema(5) reclaim was +2.8% (mean +2.7%), most of which happens in the first 3-4 sessions, so waiting longer trades a small amount of extra upside for a large amount of extra exposure to the move failing. This is a high win-rate, small-average-win system by design, which is precisely the profile a single oversized loss can erase, so the stop is sized deliberately wider than the typical adverse move (median intra-hold drawdown was -3.6%, so a 7% stop is roughly twice the typical noise) rather than tight to the entry, and a 5% take-profit locks in the strong minority of bounces before they have a chance to round-trip.
card.entry: rsi(3) < 15 and close < bb_lower(10,2)

card.display_name: H - Trend, cross-asset: lowest drawdown of the trend family
card.thesis: Round 1 forced this discipline into one sector; round 2 lets me test its central weakness directly -- trend following's worst outcome is not a bad trade, it is every position turning at once, which is a correlation problem before it is a signal problem. I measured correlation rather than assumed it. Trailing 2y (504-session) daily-return correlation across my round-1 universe (NVDA AVGO TSM ORCL SOXX NFLX MU META QCOM) averages 0.501 pairwise (median 0.468, range 0.219-0.800) through 2026-02-13 -- nine names sharing one regime. The round-2 roster this card actually trades (NVDA MU GDX EWZ FXI INDA DBC) averages 0.274 pairwise over the same window, a ~45% reduction, with every pair outside the NVDA/MU core below 0.39 and GDX the most decoupled name in the set (0.16-0.22 vs NVDA/MU). But correlation alone is not sufficient, and I tested that too: I ran the identical unscaled rule (close>sma(200) & ema(20)-crosses-above-ema(50) entry, ema(20)-crosses-below-ema(50) exit, 12% stop, 120-day time stop -- same parameters as my round-1 card, same trailing ~1500-session/6y design methodology) on every 'obvious diversifier' round 2 exposes. Bonds (TLT, mean trade return -1.6% over 5 trades), utilities (XLU, -0.5% over 18 trades), regional banks (KRE, -0.8%), biotech (XBI, -0.2%), copper (CPER, -1.1%) and defence (ITA, +2.2% mean but only 28.6% win rate, and 0.53 correlated to the semis sleeve -- a worse diversifier than gold despite the label) all showed flat-to-negative or too-thin edge under this exact rule to earn a slot: including them would not have reduced correlated drawdown, it would have parked capital in dead-or-negative-expectancy positions that still occasionally fire a badly-timed entry. Gold miners (GDX) were the standout: 4 trades in 6y, 75% win rate, +20.9% mean trade return, lowest correlation to the core of anything tested. Brazil (EWZ, +2.1% mean trade, 0.23-0.30 corr), China (FXI, +2.8%, 0.24-0.31 corr), India (INDA, +4.5%, 0.21-0.26 corr, only 0.07 correlated to DBC) and broad commodities (DBC, +5.5%, 0.07-0.39 corr) all cleared a lower but genuinely positive bar and are the five diversifying sleeves in this universe. NVDA and MU stay as the trend engine because that is where the measured edge is largest -- +17.3% and +20.6% mean trade return respectively in the same 6y window, against +12.7% averaged across all nine round-1 names and +9.7% averaged across this seven-name diversified book. The mechanism is unchanged from round 1: gradual institutional flow into a confirmed uptrend, plus both premature profit-taking and panicked pullback-selling handing the rest of a move to a slower, rule-following holder -- but now spread across sleeves whose macro drivers are structurally different (US AI capex cycle, gold's real-rate/dollar cycle, EM equity flows, broad commodity demand), so a single regime turning cannot take out the whole book the way it structurally can in a one-sector universe. This is a real trade-off, not a free lunch: the diversified book's measured per-trade expectancy (9.7%) is lower than the concentrated book's (12.7%) on this identical rule and sample -- I am spending some expected return to buy a reduction in simultaneous-drawdown risk, and round 1 is the direct comparison for whether that trade was worth it. Realised 2y annualised volatility on this universe ranges from INDA (14.1%) to MU (60.0%), a 4.3x spread wider than round 1's uniformly high-vol semis cluster, exactly as the brief warned. I did not rescale the single 12% stop because the engine cannot: it is proportionately tight on NVDA/MU (12.5%-25% measured stop-hit rate in the design window) and proportionately loose on INDA/DBC/EWZ/FXI (0% measured stop-hit rate over the same window) -- I am stating that mismatch rather than pretending a single number fits both a 60%-vol stock and a 14%-vol commodity ETF equally well.
card.entry: close > sma(200) and ema(20) crosses_above ema(50)

card.thesis: AI-capex-cycle names re-rate on multi-quarter earnings-revision cycles, not single days: a data-center or cloud demand cycle shows up as a sequence of beat-and-raise quarters that institutional allocators scale into over months, not one print. That flow creates serial correlation in price that a same-day oscillator cannot see. The other side of the trade is investors who sell into strength too early, anchored to a pre-cycle 'fair value', and investors who panic-sell the first pullback inside an intact uptrend, mistaking noise for reversal -- both hand the rest of the move to a slower, rule-following holder. I measured this rather than assuming it: on this universe's last ~1500 sessions (~6y) through 2026-02-13, a close>sma(200) regime filter plus a 20/50-EMA crossover trigger produced 77 trades at 49.4% win rate, but average winners (+29.6%) were 4.1x average losers (-7.3%), and winning trades were held a median of 118 days vs 16 for losers -- the classic trend signature of a system that is right less than half the time and still profitable because it cuts losses fast and lets the rest run. The chop problem is real and I confronted it directly: the same golden-cross setup on this universe's smaller, more speculative names (IREN, OKLO, APLD, BE, KORU) produced negative average 60-day forward returns after the signal fired -- those names were excluded from the universe below specifically because the measured data showed the entries do not sustain here, not because of a prior. Within the chosen universe, widening the stop from 8% to 12% cut stop-outs from 12/77 (16%) to 7/77 (9%) while barely moving mean trade return (0.093->0.093), meaning most of the discarded stop-outs at the tighter level were noise, not real breakdowns -- direct evidence the wider stop survives chop without giving back the move. The regime filter (sma200) plus a medium-term trigger (ema20/50, not raw ema50/200) was chosen over a textbook dual-moving-average cross because it produces materially fewer whipsaw entries on this universe's large, liquid AI/semi/software names, at the cost of entering somewhat later into each trend.
card.entry: close > sma(200) and ema(20) crosses_above ema(50)

card.thesis: In heavily-optioned, high-open-interest instruments (broad index ETFs and major sector SPDRs), a period of contracting realized volatility is systematically accompanied by net-short-gamma positioning among option sellers -- covered-call overlay funds, options-income strategies, and dealer desks that have sold volatility into the calm and hedge by trading against price. While the range holds, that flow is stabilizing: dealers buy dips and sell rips, compressing range further. When price finally closes outside the upper band while realized volatility (ATR-14) is still below its own longer-run baseline (ATR-50), the move has started before the option-selling crowd has repriced -- their short-gamma hedging flips from stabilizing to reinforcing (short calls forces the dealer/writer to buy into the breakout to stay hedged), mechanically extending the initial move for a period afterward. The other side of this trade is the option seller who wrote premium assuming continued range-bound behavior and is now a forced, mechanical buyer. What is expected to go wrong: this mechanism is about the first burst of a volatility regime change, not persistence. In a slow grinding bear (rate-driven, low realized-vol decline) there may be few or no valid low-ATR breakouts to trade, and the strategy should sit mostly in cash -- underperforming a benchmark that keeps drifting down slowly without ever tripping the squeeze condition. It is also vulnerable to a crash that gaps straight through the band with ATR already elevated (already-expanded, not compressed, volatility) -- COVID's opening days looked like that -- in which case the squeeze filter correctly refuses the entry, but a separate, unfiltered breakout would have caught the early down-move it is not designed to catch (this strategy is long-only).
card.entry: close crosses_above bb_upper(20,2.0) and atr(14) < atr(50)

card.thesis: The 200-day moving average is not a statistical artifact -- it is a level thousands of participants mechanically watch and react to at the same time (managed-futures CTAs, trend-following mutual funds, and technically-oriented traders all use variants of it), so a break of it triggers correlated follow-on flow rather than random noise. The other side of the trade is supplied by participants who are slow or unwilling to move: index funds and 401k flows that buy/sell on a schedule unrelated to price level, and holders exhibiting the disposition effect who keep underwater positions past the point a trend-follower would already have exited, cushioning the trend-follower's fills. Applying the identical rule independently across three assets whose price drivers are structurally different (US equity beta, long-duration interest-rate risk, and a non-yielding hard asset with its own supply/demand book) means the three trend signals are not forced to fire together -- when equity trend breaks down in a genuine flight-to-quality event, rate or gold trend can still be up, which a single-asset or single-sector trend book cannot offer. This is not a hedge (the rules do not compare symbols to each other -- the engine cannot do that); it is three independent bets whose bad years are not the same years, which the correlation numbers in the memo support. What I expect to go wrong: fast V-shaped shocks. A 200-day average reacts on the order of weeks, not days, so a crash-and-snapback that completes inside a single quarter (COVID is the designed example) will be entered late on the way down and re-entered late on the way back up, capturing the worst of both transitions rather than avoiding them.
card.entry: close crosses_above sma(200)
